AFG: Almost six times the size of Virginia and slightly smaller than Texas.
Afghanistan had more changes to its national flag in the 20th century than any other country, 19 by one count.
The suffix "-stan" means "place of" or "country," so Afghanistan literally means the "Land of the Afghans".
The Hindu Kush divides the northern provinces from the rest of the country; the highest peaks lie in the Wakhan Corridor.
The Taliban took over Afghanistan on 15 August 2021; to date, no country has recognized it as the government.
Afghanistan had 5,457,183 internally displaced persons in 2024, by Factbook estimate.
ALB: Albania is slightly smaller than Maryland.
The local name Shqiperia is popularly interpreted to mean "Land of the Eagles".
Lake Scutari, shared with Montenegro, is the largest lake in the Balkans at 400 sq km.
Only the first two stanzas of the original poem are used in the anthem "Hymni i Flamurit".
In 1999, some 450,000 ethnic Albanians fled from Kosovo to Albania to escape the war with the Serbs.
The flag's design is said to come from 15th-century hero Skanderbeg, who led a successful uprising against the Ottoman Turks.
DZA: Algeria is slightly less than 3.5 times the size of Texas.
The flag's crescent is more closed than most because Algerians believe the long crescent horns bring happiness.
Prehistoric rock art in Tassili n'Ajjer depicts elephants and giraffes from roughly 5,000 to 11,000 years ago, when the region was vegetated.
Mufdi Zakariah wrote the anthem "Kassaman" (We Pledge) as a poem while imprisoned in Algiers.
The French captured Algiers in 1830; a bloody eight-year struggle culminated in Algerian independence in 1962.
Military spending reached 8% of GDP in 2024, up from 4.8% in 2022.
ASM: Pago Pago has one of the best natural deepwater harbors in the South Pacific Ocean.
A bald eagle on the flag holds a Samoan war club and a coconut-fiber fly whisk, traditional symbols of authority.
By one theory, sa means "sacred" and moa means "center," so the name can mean "Holy Center."
American Samoa remains an unorganized territory, and people born there are US nationals rather than US citizens.
AND: Andorra is 2.5 times the size of Washington, D.C.
The national symbol is a red cow, breed unspecified.
Even the lowest point, Riu Runer, sits at 840 m; the mean elevation is 1,996 m.
Andorra's anthem, "El Gran Carlemany," tells a brief history of the country in a first-person narrative.
For 715 years, from 1278 to 1993, Andorrans lived under a co-principality ruled by French and Spanish leaders.
Andorra's defense is the responsibility of France and Spain.
AGO: The province of Cabinda is an exclave, separated from the rest of Angola by the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
In the 15th century, Portuguese explorers derived the name from "N'gola," a title held by kings of the Ndongo.
The national symbol is the giant black sable antelope, or Palanca negra gigante.
About eight times the size of Georgia and slightly less than twice the size of Texas.
Up to 1.5 million lives may have been lost in the civil war, a major Cold War conflict that lasted more than a quarter-century.
The flag's emblem, a star inside half a cogwheel crossed by a machete, is styled after the hammer and sickle.
AIA: Columbus named the island Anguilla, Spanish for "eel," in 1493 because of its elongated shape.
Anguilla is the most northerly of the Leeward Islands in the Lesser Antilles.
Three orange dolphins on the coat of arms stand for endurance, unity, and strength.
About one-half the size of Washington, D.C.
Anguilla was finally allowed to secede from its union with Saint Kitts and Nevis in 1971, two years after a revolt.
ATA: In summer, more solar radiation reaches the surface at the South Pole than the equator receives in an equivalent period.
Denman Glacier, the lowest point, lies more than 3,500 m below sea level.
The name comes from the Greek anti and arktikos, meaning "opposite to the Arctic."
The unofficial True South flag, created in 2018, shows a peak casting a shadow shaped like a compass arrow pointed south.
Seven countries have made territorial claims here; most countries do not recognize them, and the Antarctic Treaty neither denies nor recognizes them.
The Antarctic Treaty bans military bases, maneuvers, and weapons testing, but allows military personnel for science and other peaceful purposes.
ATG: The name Antigua honors the church of Santa Maria la Antigua (Old Saint Mary's) in Seville, Spain.
The highest point is Mount Obama, at 402 m.
Yellow, blue, and white on the flag are meant to evoke the tourist attractions of sun, sea, and sand.
Its one World Heritage Site is Antigua Naval Dockyard, also known as Nelson's Dockyard.
Slavery, which provided the labor on Antigua's sugar plantations, was abolished in 1834.
Created in 1981 from colonial forces first formed in 1897, its defense force is one of the world's smallest militaries.
ARG: Argentina holds both the Western Hemisphere's tallest mountain, Cerro Aconcagua, and its lowest point, Laguna del Carbon.
The Sun of May on the flag is designed to look like Inti, the Incan god of the sun.
The name derives from a Spanish word for "silver" and may refer to the Rio de la Plata, or "Silver River."
Of the anthem's original nine verses, only the first and last were declared official by a 1900 presidential decree.
In 1982, Argentina's military junta failed in its bid to seize the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) by force from the UK.
The military staged coups in 1930, 1943, 1955, 1962, 1966, and 1976, the last beginning the so-called "Dirty War."
ARM: Armenia prides itself on being the first state to formally adopt Christianity, in the early 4th century.
By tradition, the local name Hayastan comes from Hayk, legendary patriarch of the Armenians and great-great-grandson of Noah.
Landlocked in the Lesser Caucasus, Armenia holds Lake Sevan, the largest lake in that mountain range.
The orange band on the flag stands for the land and the courage of the workers who farm it.
In World War I, Ottoman forced resettlement caused at least 1 million Armenian deaths, widely recognized as genocide.
Armenia joined both the Russian-led CSTO and NATO's Partnership for Peace program in 1994.
ABW: Tradition says the name comes from the Spanish oro hubo ("there was gold"), but no gold was ever found on the island.
A flat, riverless island where the temperature is almost constant at about 27 degrees Celsius.
The four points of the flag's red star stand for the major languages and the points of a compass.
Aruba lies outside the Caribbean hurricane belt and is rarely threatened.
Aruba seceded from the Netherlands Antilles in 1986; its movement toward full independence was halted at its own request in 1990.
ATC: About eight times the size of the National Mall in Washington, D.C.
Named after Captain Samuel Ashmore, who sighted one island in 1811, and the ship Cartier, which found the other in 1800.
The highest point, on Cartier Island, is just 5 m.
Ashmore Reef National Nature Reserve was established in 1983.
A 1974 Australia-Indonesia agreement lets Indonesian fishermen keep fishing around the islands and visit the graves of past fishermen.
AUS: The world's smallest continent is also the sixth-largest country and the largest country without land borders.
The name comes from the Latin australis, meaning "southern"; the landmass was long called Terra Australis.
The flag's seven-pointed Commonwealth Star has a point for each of the six original states and one for the territories.
Australia has 21 World Heritage Sites, among them the Great Barrier Reef and the Sydney Opera House.
Settlement, disease, and the forced removal of children cut the Aboriginal population from over 700,000 to a low of 74,000 in 1933.
Australian and US forces first fought together in France in 1918 and have fought together in every major US conflict since.
AUT: Eisriesenwelt, near Werfen, is the world's largest and longest ice cave system at 42 km.
Austria's red-white-red flag is one of the oldest national flags in the world.
The name Oesterreich means "eastern realm" and dates to the 10th century.
Authorship of the anthem's music is disputed between Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Johann Holzer.
A 1955 State Treaty ended the Allied occupation, recognized Austria's independence, and forbade unification with Germany.
Austria replaced its Haydn imperial anthem after World War II; Germany had appropriated it in 1922, and it became associated with the Nazis.
AZE: The name can be translated as "Fire Keeper" or "The Land of Fire," from the local word azer, meaning fire.
The eight points of the flag's star represent the eight Turkic peoples of the world.
Both the main area of the country and the Naxcivan exclave are landlocked.
"March of Azerbaijan" was written in 1919 but did not become the official anthem until after the Soviet Union dissolved.
In September 2023, Azerbaijan took military action to regain Nagorno-Karabakh; nearly its entire ethnic Armenian population fled.
Azerbaijan had 657,996 internally displaced persons in 2024 (est.).
BHS: The name may come from the Spanish baha mar, "low sea," describing the shallow waters of the Bahama Banks.
The highest point, just 64 m, lies 1.3 km NE of Old Bight on Cat Island.
Of its extensive island chain, 30 islands are inhabited.
Aquamarine bands on the flag represent the sea surrounding the islands' golden beaches.
Piracy thrived here in the 17th and 18th centuries because the islands lay close to shipping lanes.
BHR: Bahrain means "the two seas" in Arabic, referring to the water bodies on each side of the archipelago.
Until 2002 the flag had eight white points; they were cut to five to avoid confusion with the Qatari flag.
About 3.5 times the size of Washington, D.C.
The highest point, Jabal ad Dukhan, rises just 135 m.
Bahrain hosts the US Naval Forces Central Command, which includes the US 5th Fleet.
Bahrainis make up 47.4% of the population, nearly matched by Asians at 43.4% (2020 est.).
BGD: The anthem's author, Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore, also wrote India's national anthem.
The name combines the Bengali words Bangla (Bengali) and desh (country).
Most of the country sits on deltas of large rivers flowing from the Himalayas, which empty into the Bay of Bengal.
Slightly larger than Pennsylvania and New Jersey combined; slightly smaller than Iowa.
After partition in 1947, the area became East Pakistan; an India-supported movement won Bangladesh's independence war in 1971.
Bangladesh hosted 1,005,637 refugees and 1,005,520 stateless persons in 2024 (est.).
BRB: Barbados means "the bearded ones," perhaps for the beard-like leaves of the island's fig trees.
Barbados is the easternmost Caribbean island.
A black trident head on the flag represents independence and a break with the past.
Among its national symbols is the red bird of paradise flower, also known as "Pride of Barbados."
Barbados became a republic in 2021, with former Governor-General Sandra Mason elected as its first president.
BLR: Glacial scouring accounts for the flatness of Belarus and for its 11,000 lakes.
The name combines the Slavic "bel" (white) and "Rus" to mean White Rusian or White Ruthenian.
Belarus kept the music of its Soviet-era anthem but adopted new lyrics in 2002.
The highest point, Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, reaches 346 m; the mean elevation is 160 m.
In 2023, Belarus agreed to permit Russia to deploy nuclear weapons on its soil.
Alyaksandr Lukashenka, in office since 1994, is the country's first and only directly elected president.
BEL: Most West European capitals are within 1,000 km of Brussels, the seat of both the EU and NATO.
The flag's colors come from the arms of Brabant: a yellow lion with red claws and tongue on black.
Legend says the anthem's lyrics were written by an actor with a group of young people in a Brussels cafe.
The name derives from the Belgae, an ancient Celtic tribal confederation.
Belgium became independent from the Netherlands in 1830 and was occupied by Germany during both World Wars.
Belgium was one of the original 12 countries to sign the North Atlantic Treaty, which established NATO in 1949.
BLZ: Belize is the only country in Central America without a coastline on the North Pacific Ocean.
Tradition holds that the name comes from the Spanish pronunciation of Scottish explorer Peter Wallace's last name.
A garland of 50 mahogany leaves rings the coat of arms on the flag.
Baird's tapir, a large forest-dwelling mammal, is a national symbol alongside the keel-billed toucan.
Territorial disputes between the UK and Guatemala delayed independence until 1981, and Guatemala refused to recognize Belize until 1992.
The British Army has kept a presence since independence: a small unit giving jungle training to UK and partner troops.
BEN: The former name, Dahomey, comes from Dan Homé, a previous kingdom in the area.
Sandbanks make the coast hard to reach, and it has no natural harbors, river mouths, or islands.
Benin is slightly smaller than Pennsylvania.
The leopard is the national symbol of Benin.
Free elections in 1991 marked the first successful transfer of power in Africa from a dictatorship to a democracy.
Vodoun is practiced by 11.6% of people, alongside Muslims at 27.7% and Roman Catholics at 25.5% (2013 est.).
BMU: Over 170 coral islands and islets with ample rainfall, but no rivers or freshwater lakes.
Named after Juan de Bermudez, a 16th-century Spanish sea captain and the first European to explore the archipelago.
The lion on the coat of arms holds a scroll showing the 1609 wreck of the Sea Venture, which led to Bermuda's settling.
Its World Heritage Site is the Historic Town of St. George and Related Fortifications.
Self-governing since 1620, Bermuda soundly defeated independence from the UK in a 1995 referendum.
BTN: Violent storms from the Himalayas are the source of the Bhutanese name, which translates as Land of the Thunder Dragon.
The name may come from Sanskrit bhoṭa (Tibet) and anta (end), for its place at the southernmost end of Tibet.
The flag's dragon, the Druk or Thunder Dragon, holds jewels in its claws that symbolize wealth.
Elevation climbs from 97 m at Drangeme Chhu to 7,570 m at Gangkar Puensum.
Over 100,000 ethnic Nepali refugees fled or were forced out of Bhutan in the 1990s; as of 2024, about 6,500 remain displaced in Nepal.
Militia training is compulsory for Bhutanese men aged 20-25, over a 3-year period.
BOL: Bolivia shares control of Lago Titicaca, the world's highest navigable lake at 3,805 m, with Peru.
Since 2009, a wiphala, a square multi-colored flag, must be used alongside the national flag.
National symbols include the llama, the Andean condor, and two national flowers, the cantuta and the patuju.
Once called Upper Peru, the country is named in honor of Simon Bolivar, a leader in the wars for independence.
Landlocked Bolivia keeps a navy, partly as a reminder of its defeat by Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879-1883).
Much of Bolivia's history after 1825 was a series of coups and countercoups, the last in 1980.
BIH: The anthem remains officially wordless; lyrics proposed in 2009 are still awaiting adoption.
The yellow triangle on the flag approximates the country's shape.
Herzegovina comes from the Old Serbian word herceg, "duke," to denote a "dukedom".
Bosnia and Herzegovina has just 20 km of coastline.
From 1992 to 1995, ethnic cleansing campaigns killed thousands and displaced more than two million people.
The three points of the flag's yellow triangle stand for the Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs.
BWA: The Kalahari Desert covers about 70% of the country, while the Okavango Delta is one of the largest inland deltas in the world.
On the flag, blue symbolizes rainwater, and the black and white bands represent racial harmony.
Botswana's border with Zambia is just 0.15 km long.
Botswana means "Land of the Tswana"; the country was formerly called Bechuanaland.
In 1852, Tswana forces halted white Afrikaner settlers seeking to expand their territory northward into what is now Botswana.
There was no permanent military under British rule; the Botswana Defense Force was only established in 1977.
BRA: Brazil shares boundaries with every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
The stars on the flag depict the sky over Rio de Janeiro on the morning of 15 November 1889.
The name comes from the brazil tree, which once grew plentifully along the coast and was used for a deep red dye.
The national symbol is the Southern Cross constellation.
Brazil kept a monarchy until slavery was abolished in 1888; the military proclaimed a republic in 1889.
Brazil sent a 25,000-man expeditionary force to fight with the Allies in the Mediterranean during World War II.
IOT: The territory has no natural hazards and lies outside the routes of Indian Ocean cyclones.
An archipelago of 55 islands, of which only Diego Garcia is inhabited.
Six wavy blue stripes on the flag represent the Indian Ocean and may stand for the six main atolls.
Most areas of these flat, low coral atolls do not exceed 2 m in elevation.
Between 1967 and 1973 the islanders, known as Chagossians, were relocated, primarily to Mauritius but also to the Seychelles.
A 2025 agreement will transfer the Chagos Archipelago to Mauritius, with the UK leasing Diego Garcia and its UK-US base for 99 years.
VGB: The islets reminded Columbus of Saint Ursula and her 11,000 virgin followers, a name later shortened to the Virgins.
The coat of arms shows Saint Ursula between columns of oil lamps, above the Latin word VIGILATE (Be Watchful).
National symbols are the zenaida dove and the white cedar flower.
Mount Sage is the highest point, at 521 m.
BRN: The eastern Temburong district is an exclave and almost an enclave within Malaysia.
The same family has ruled Brunei for over six centuries.
A ribbon on the flag's emblem reads "Brunei, the Abode of Peace".
The national symbol is the royal parasol.
Brunei hosts a British Army garrison that includes a Gurkha battalion and a jungle warfare school.
BGR: Bulgaria is almost identical in size to Virginia.
The Bulgar tribal name may come from the Turkic word bulga, meaning "mixed".
First adopted in 1879, the flag was a modified Russian tricolor, using green instead of blue.
Bulgaria has 10 World Heritage Sites, including Rila Monastery and the Madara Rider.
The anthem "Mila Rodino" was composed in 1885 by a student on his way to fight in the Serbo-Bulgarian War.
During the Cold War, Bulgaria had one of the Warsaw Pact's largest militaries, with over 150,000 personnel.
BFA: The name translates as "Land of the Worthy Men," from the Dyula words burkina (worthy) and faso (land).
The anthem was written by former president Thomas Sankara, an avid guitar player.
This landlocked savanna is cut by three principal rivers: the Black, Red, and White Voltas.
A white stallion is the national symbol.
The armed forces have conducted eight coups since their formation in 1960-61, the most recent in September 2022.
An estimated 2,065,358 people were internally displaced within the country in 2024.
BDI: Burundi straddles the crest of the Nile-Congo watershed; the Kagera is the most remote headstream of the White Nile.
The name comes from the Rundi or Barundi people; ba- is the prefix for the people and bu- for the country.
Lake Tanganyika, shared with the Democratic Republic of Congo, Tanzania, and Zambia, covers 32,000 sq km.
Burundi is slightly smaller than Maryland.
The flag's three red stars represent the major ethnic groups, Hutu, Twa, and Tutsi, as well as unity, work, and progress.
The accords that ended the 1993-2005 civil war required the military to have a 50/50 ethnic mix of Tutsis and Hutus.
KHM: Tonle Sap lake covers anywhere from 2,700 to 16,000 sq km.
A stylized three-towered white temple representing Angkor Wat sits at the center of the flag.
The name is derived from Kambu, a legendary ancestor of the Cambodian people.
National symbols are the Angkor Wat temple and the kouprey, a wild ox.
At least 1.5 million Cambodians died from execution, forced hardships, or starvation under the Khmer Rouge regime of Pol Pot.
One World Heritage listing is the Cambodian Memorial Sites: from centres of repression to places of peace and reflection.
CMR: Portuguese explorers named an estuary Rio dos Camaroes (River of Prawns) for its shrimp, a name that evolved into Cameroon.
Sometimes called the hinge of Africa for its central location at the west-south juncture of the Gulf of Guinea.
Fako on Mont Cameroun, at 4,045 m, is the highest point.
Lake Chad's area varies by season and year to year, from 10,360 to 25,900 sq km.
After World War I, the German colony of Kamerun was divided between France and the UK as League of Nations mandates.
Religion splits roughly three ways: Roman Catholic 33.1%, Muslim 30.6%, and Protestant 27.1% (2022 est.).
CAN: Canada has at least 2 million and possibly over 3 million lakes, more than all other countries combined.
Its land border with Denmark (Greenland) measures just 1.3 km.
The name probably comes from the Huron or Iroquois word kanata, meaning village or camp.
One of its 22 World Heritage Sites is Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump.
More than 425,000 Canadian soldiers went to Europe in World War I as the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
An estimated 561,551 refugees were living in Canada in 2024.
CPV: The name derives from the Cape Verde (Green Cape) peninsula on the Senegalese coast, the westernmost point of Africa.
One of four North Atlantic archipelagos that make up Macaronesia, with the Azores, Canary Islands, and Madeira.
The flag's circle of 10 yellow stars represents the 10 major islands.
Mt. Fogo, a volcano on Fogo Island, is the highest point at 2,829 m.
Uninhabited when the Portuguese colonized them in the 15th century, the islands became a trading center for African slaves.
CYM: Spanish explorers named the islands with the Carib word for marine crocodiles, caiman.
A pineapple on the coat of arms represents ties to Jamaica; a turtle, the islands' seafaring tradition.
The green sea turtle is the national symbol.
The highest point, 1 km southwest of The Bluff on Cayman Brac, is only 50 m.
Cayman Islanders make up 35.4% of the population, followed by Jamaicans at 24.8% (2021 est.).
CAF: Landlocked and almost the precise center of Africa.
"Africa" derives from the Roman "Africa terra," meaning "Land of the Afri," in present-day Tunisia.
Barthelemy Boganda, who wrote the anthem's lyrics, was the first prime minister of the autonomous French territory.
Slightly smaller than Texas and about four times the size of Georgia.
In 1976, Jean-Bedel Bokassa named himself emperor and changed the country's name to the Central African Empire.
The 2013 coup caused the army's institutional collapse; it has been estimated that only 10% of its forces returned afterward.
TCD: At its greatest extent, paleolake Mega-Chad covered about 400,000 sq km, roughly the size of today's Caspian Sea.
A local word meaning "large body of water" or "lake" gave Lake Chad its name, and the country is named for the lake.
Chad has two national symbols: the goat in the north and the lion in the south.
Almost nine times the size of New York state and slightly more than three times the size of California.
The 1987 "Toyota War" that expelled Libyan forces was named for the Toyota pickup trucks used as fighting vehicles.
An estimated 1,286,645 refugees were in Chad in 2024, and 1,542,532 people were internally displaced.
CHL: Chile is the longest country north-to-south in the world, extending across 39 degrees of latitude.
Nevado Ojos del Salado, at 6,893 m, is the highest volcano in the world.
The name may come from a local word meaning "land's end" or "cold," or one confused with chili, for the area's shape.
The huemul, a mountain deer, is a national symbol along with the Andean condor.
Under Pinochet's military rule, a verse glorifying the army was added to the anthem; it was removed when democracy returned in 1990.
In the War of the Pacific (1879-83), Chile defeated Peru and Bolivia to win its current northernmost regions.
CHN: The Miao Room in the Gebihe cave system is the largest cave chamber in the world.
Elevation spans from 8,849 m atop Mount Everest to 154 m below sea level in the Turpan Pendi (Turfan Depression).
The Chinese name Zhongguo translates as "Central Nation" or "Middle Country".
China has 60 World Heritage Sites, among them the Great Wall and the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor.
Japan's full-scale invasion in 1937 began eight years of warfare that cost up to 20 million Chinese lives.
The People's Liberation Army is the world's largest military; the China Coast Guard is the largest maritime law enforcement fleet.
IOA: Christmas Island was named for the day of its rediscovery, Christmas Day, 25 December 1643.
Of the 27 Cocos coral islands, all but North Keeling form a horseshoe-shaped atoll around a lagoon.
Christmas Island has 18 km of standard gauge railway, not in operation.
Christmas Island's flag shows a golden bosun bird and a yellow disk with a green outline of the island.
In 2001 Australia declared Christmas Island outside its migration zone and built an immigration detention center there.
The Clunies-Ross family ruled the Cocos Islands in a feudal style until 1978, when Australia bought all the land they held.
COL: Colombia is the only South American country with coastlines on both the North Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.
The country is named after explorer Christopher Columbus.
The anthem comes from a poem by President Rafael Nunez and always starts with the chorus.
The Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia is one of 9 World Heritage Sites.
An estimated 7,264,767 people were internally displaced in Colombia in 2024.
After four years of formal talks, the government signed a final peace accord with the FARC in 2016.
COM: The name derives from the Arabic al qamar, meaning the moon.
The only Arab League country that lies entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.
Comoros is slightly more than 12 times the size of Washington, D.C.
Karthala, at 2,360 m, is the highest point.
Since independence in 1975, Comoros has weathered approximately 20 successful and attempted coups, mostly before 2000.
One of the flag's four stars represents Mahore (Mayotte), which is a department of France but claimed by Comoros.
COG: About 70% of the population lives in Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire, or along the railroad between them.
Named for the Congo River, whose name derives from Kongo, a Bantu kingdom in the area.
"La Congolaise" was originally adopted as the anthem in 1959 and restored in 1991.
Slightly smaller than Montana and about twice the size of Florida.
A quarter-century of experimentation with Marxism was abandoned in 1990; from 1968 to 1992 it was the People's Republic of the Congo.
During the 1997-1999 civil war, most northern officers backed Sassou-Nguesso, while most southerners backed the rebels.
COK: Named after Captain James Cook, who visited in 1773 and 1777; the former name was the Hervey Islands.
A circle of 15 white stars on the flag has one star for each island.
Rarotonga, the largest island, covers just 67 sq km.
The tiare maori flower (Gardenia taitensis) is a national symbol.
In September 2023 the US recognized the Cook Islands, in free association with New Zealand, as a sovereign and independent state.
CRI: Costa Rica means "rich coast" in Spanish, a name Columbus gave in 1502 for its abundant vegetation and water.
A red stripe was added to the flag in 1848 to incorporate the French colors, in response to revolutions in Europe.
The anthem's music was first written for an 1852 welcome ceremony for the US and UK diplomatic missions.
Rugged mountains here include over 100 volcanic cones, several of them major active volcanoes.
In 1948, landowner Jose Figueres Ferrer raised his own army and rebelled against the government in a brief civil war.
Costa Rica was home to an estimated 249,521 refugees in 2024.
CIV: The French version of the name has been used internationally since 1986, at the country's request.
The anthem, "L'Abidjanaise" (Song of Abidjan), is named after the former capital city of Abidjan.
On the flag, orange stands for the savannah, white for peace and unity, and green for the forests of the south.
Côte d'Ivoire is slightly larger than New Mexico.
A 2003 cease-fire left rebels holding the north, the government the south, and peacekeepers occupying a buffer zone in the middle.
An estimated 930,978 people in Côte d'Ivoire were stateless in 2024.
HRV: Some 1,200 islands, islets, ridges, and rocks lie off the coast of Croatia.
The coat of arms on the flag has a checkerboard of 13 red and 12 silver fields.
Written in 1835, the lyrics of "Lijepa nasa domovino" served as an unofficial anthem from 1891.
The Croats' name may be related to the Russian word khrebet, meaning "mountain chain".
Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, but it took four years of fighting before Yugoslav forces were cleared from its lands.
Croatia abolished conscription in 2008; it is to be reinstated in 2026 as two months of basic training for men aged 19-29.
CUB: Cuba is the largest country in the Caribbean and the westernmost island of the Greater Antilles.
The flag's white star, "La Estrella Solitaria" (the Lone Star), was inspired by the state flag of Texas.
The name may come from the Taino cubao, "where fertile land is abundant," or coabana, "great place."
Pico Turquino, at 1,974 m, is the highest point.
Anthem author Pedro Figueredo, captured in 1870 and shot by firing squad, is said to have cried its line "To die for the country is to live."
Cuba's only land boundary is a 28.5 km line with the US Naval Base at Guantanamo Bay.
CUW: The two stars on the flag stand for Curaçao and its uninhabited sister island, Klein Curaçao.
The lyrics of "Himmo di Korsou," first written in 1899, were rewritten in 1978 to remove colonial references.
Semiarid, with average rainfall of 60 cm a year.
The laraha, a citrus tree, is the national symbol.
Once the center of the Caribbean slave trade, Curaçao was hit hard economically when the Dutch abolished slavery in 1863.
CYP: Cyprus is the third largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, after Sicily and Sardinia.
The Greek name Kupros probably derives from the Sumerian kabar, meaning "copper" or "bronze".
A copper-colored silhouette of the island sits above two crossed green olive branches on the flag.
The Cypriot mouflon, a wild sheep, is a national symbol alongside the white dove.
In 1983, the Turkish Cypriot-administered area declared itself the "Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus," recognized only by Turkey.
Cyprus uses the Greek national anthem, while the Turkish Cypriot community uses Turkey's.
CZE: The Hranice Abyss is the world's deepest surveyed freshwater cave at 519 m, and its survey is not complete.
The anthem "Kde domov muj?" began as incidental music for the 1834 play "Fidlovacka".
The national symbol is a silver (or white) double-tailed rampant lion.
The Labe (Elbe) River rises in Czechia and flows 1,252 km to its mouth in Germany.
In 1968, an invasion by fellow Warsaw Pact troops ended the leaders' efforts to create "socialism with a human face".
In Czechia, 47.8% report no religion and 7% are Roman Catholic (2021 est.).
DNK: Besides its 140 km border with Germany, Denmark has a 1.3 km land border with Canada.
